pr_title: kubelet(OOM-score-adj): change OOM score adjustment calculation for sidecar container
pr_body:
/kind feature
/sig node
/triage accepted


#### What this PR does / why we need it:
calculate the sidecar oom score adjustment based on: max-memory( currentSideCarContainer , min -memory(regular containers) ) .

the OOM adjustment for these containers will match or fall below the OOM score adjustment of regular containers in the Pod. 


#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:
*Automatically closes linked issue when PR is merged.
Usage: `Fixes https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/111356 .


Fixes #

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
Change OOM score adjustment calculation for sidecar container : the OOM adjustment for these containers will match or fall below the OOM score adjustment of regular containers in the Pod.
```

issue_context.title: The logic of oom_score_adj doesn't work well for sidecar containers
issue_context.body:
### What happened?

I was debugging a OOM failure recently and noticed some unexpected behavior for how the kubelet is setting `oom_score_adj`.

From the [Node-pressure Eviction documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/node-pressure-eviction/) this is how setting `oom_score_adj` is described for burstable QoS pods:

> min(max(2, 1000 - (1000 * memoryRequestBytes) / machineMemoryCapacityBytes), 999)

The documentation also states the intention of this calculation is:

> This means that containers in low QoS pods that consume a large amount of memory relative to their scheduling requests are killed first.

However the calculation actually does the opposite. For processes that request a small amount of memory the `(1000 * memoryRequestBytes) / machineMemoryCapacityBytes` ratio approaches zero, meaning the calculation ends up being: `min(max(2, 1000 - 0), 999) = 999`

Similarly, when the requested memory increases and the ratio approaches the total size of the machine the calculation becomes: `min(max(2, 1000 - 1000), 999) = 2`

This means that containers that are using the smallest amount of the machine get the highest score adjustment which makes the smallest processes killed first. I observed this in practice while looking at the kernel's OOM logs. These are the set of processes the OOM killer was logging:

Due to the `999` value of `oom_score_adj` processes in the `vault` container were killed first, despite having the smallest resource request and the smallest memory footprint.

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected that containers that are using a larger portion of the machine to have `oom_score_adj` set to a higher value than containers that are using a small portion of the machine. This matches the intentions stated in the existing documentation. Changing the calculation to this should have that intended effect:

```
min(max(2, 1000 * memoryRequestBytes / machineMemoryCapacityBytes), 999)
```

With that change as the ratio of requested memory approaches the entire machine the value will approach 999, which will make the OOM killer most likely to target those processes.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a burstable QoS pod that requests and uses a small amount of memory.
2. Create a burstable pod that requests a large amount of memory and has a memory leak that will eventually trigger the OOM killer.
3. Look at the OOM killer kernel logs and see that the small pod was targeted first.

@jpinkul I think you're misinterpreting this.

The calculations you cited are done by kubernetes, and they take into account two values:
 * `memoryRequestBytes` -- this is how much memory a container _requests_ (note this is NOT the current usage and NOT the memory limit, but rather a minimally required memory for a container -- although, if unset, this defaults to limit)
 * `machineMemoryCapacityBytes` -- this is basically how much memory the server has
 
Based on these two values, OOM score _adjustment_ is calculated and set.
 
Now, when OOM killer is invoked, it uses a _container_'s memory limit as well as a _process's_ (not container's) current memory usage to calculate OOM _score_ (not the _score adjustment_). Processes that are over the container's cgroup limit will have the score of 1000. Than the adjustment is applied.

Note that some containers may run a single process, while some others may run multiple small processes, and they are treated by the OOM killer separately (unless for cgroup v2, when `memory.oom.group == 1`, which apparently is never the case with k8s since by default `memory.oom.group = 0`, and also most people still use cgroup v1).

The code in question was written in 2015 and is reviewed in #12182. The idea behind the adjustment is described here:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d6a3a68afce1525dc31a2a8e73a2bc5903120eb9/pkg/kubelet/qos/policy.go#L54-L61

As a result, this code gives the following OOM score _adjustments_:
 * 3 to processes inside a container which _requests_ 100% of memory
 * 500 to processes inside a container which _requests_ 50% of memory
 * 900 to processes inside a container which _requests_ 10% of memory
 
Again, the OOM score is determined on a per-process basis, using the process (not the container) memory usage and the container memory limit (not the requested memory!). For example, if we have three big processes each using 10% of memory running in different containers, the one in a container with smaller memory _limit_ will have higher OOM score (before the adjustment). The end result (after the adjustment) depends on the memory _requested_ (not limited).

Now I can't say if this algorithm is good or bad, because there are too much variables involved. What I can say is your initial analysis appears to be incorrect.

Thanks for the additional context! I didn't realize how this score adjustment was intended to interact with the base OOM score.

To summarize the final OOM score consists of two components, the base OOM score which is from the actual usage of the process and the adjustment which is based off of the requested container resources. Containers that request a higher portion of a machine derive more of the final score from the usage of the process. Conversely containers that request a smaller portion of the machine derive more of the final score from the container requested memory.

This explains why I observed an OOM kill of a process that was using less memory than the container's memory request and was running in a container that had requested a small amount of memory. In this case since the ratio of the container's `memoryRequestBytes` to `machineMemoryCapacityBytes` was so small the OOM adjustment was set to the max of 999. This means that containers that request a very small portion of the machine will be targeted by the OOM killer regardless of the memory usage of their processes.

This behavior still seems undesirable since targeting these small containers causes failures without freeing a significant amount of memory. Is there a workaround to prevent these small `memoryRequestBytes` containers from being targeted? For single container pods we could use a `Guaranteed` QoS but that wouldn't work for pods that have small side cars, such as the vault injector.

/remove-kind bug
/kind feature

I think oomkilling "small" bursteable pods is a good logic in general. Those are easier to reschedule and likely will cause less interruption. They are almost best effort in oom adjustment calculations.

As for the sidecars - it is a valid point that killing small sidecars of a large pod may be more disruptive and less efficient than smaller pod or smaller pod's sidecar. In other words, maybe formulae needs to account the entire pod request. Since there is no way to tell if the container is a sidecar container, maybe some heuristic may be applied. Perhaps, use the entire pod's OOM score adjustment for the containers when those containers are requesting a fraction of memory of the entire pod's request.

I was thinking of also using `restartPolicy` to determine the right calculation, but I don't think it will be easy to tell whether a containers inside the pod are more or less OK to be OOM killed based on this policy.

/retitle The logic of oom_score_adj doesn't work well for sidecar containers
